references.text: Jacob recognizes Joseph's bloodied tunic and believes he has been killed by a wild animal – the background for the grief he expresses in Genesis 42:36.
Jacob mourns over Joseph and refuses to be comforted, showing the depth of the sorrow he still carries in Genesis 42:36.
Jacob refuses to send Benjamin to Egypt with his brothers out of fear for his safety – the same fear he expresses in Genesis 42:36.
The brothers return from Egypt and report to Jacob about the demands of Egypt's ruler, which directly leads to Jacob's complaint in Genesis 42:36.
Jacob categorically refuses to send Benjamin and fears that disaster will befall him – a direct continuation of his complaint in Genesis 42:36.
Jacob finally relents and sends Benjamin with the brothers, invoking God Almighty's mercy – following up on his desperate situation in Genesis 42:36.
Judah repeats to Joseph what their father said about losing Joseph and fearing to lose Benjamin, which directly reflects Jacob's complaint in Genesis 42:36.
A parallel lament from Jacob that sons have brought disaster and threatened the family's survival.
